questions.q: What is "source format" in the context of Salesforce DX?
options: The flatter, zip-oriented layout used by the raw Metadata API
A granular, per-component file layout with readable individual files, used by Salesforce DX projects
A proprietary binary format only readable by the Developer Console
The format change sets use to bundle metadata for deployment
questions.explain: Source format breaks metadata into a granular, readable folder structure with individual files per component, as opposed to the flatter Metadata API (mdapi) format used for raw deploy/retrieve zip calls.

questions.q: An Apex class's source-format files typically include a `.cls` file and what companion file?
options: A `.cls-meta.xml` file holding the component's metadata-only attributes
A `.cls.zip` archive
A `.cls-backup` file
No companion file is needed
questions.explain: Source format pairs each content file with a companion -meta.xml file holding that component's metadata attributes — for an Apex class, that's the .cls-meta.xml file sitting alongside the .cls file.

questions.q: In source-driven development, what does it mean to say the org "never holds information that doesn't also exist in Git"?
options: Orgs are read-only and cannot be edited at all
If a change was made directly in an org and never retrieved into the project's Git history, the project doesn't yet reflect it, as if it doesn't exist
Git automatically mirrors every org change in real time with no action needed
Orgs store a complete backup of every Git commit
questions.explain: The lesson states that from the project's point of view, an org change never retrieved into the local files and committed to Git effectively doesn't exist yet — Git, not the org, is the source of truth.

questions.q: Which of these is a genuine downside of skipping source-driven development and developing directly in shared sandboxes, per this lesson?
options: It becomes impossible to create scratch orgs
Teams tend to lose track of who changed what and struggle to reproduce bugs tied to a prior org state
Apex classes stop compiling
The Metadata API becomes unavailable
questions.explain: Without source-driven development's Git history, teams lose a reliable record of who changed what and when, making it hard to reproduce a bug tied to what the org looked like at an earlier point in time.

questions.q: Which step of the simplified day-to-day source-driven development loop described in this lesson comes last?
options: Creating a scratch org
Deploying the project's current source into the org
Committing the synced result to Git
Making a change in the org's UI or in local files
questions.explain: The loop runs: create/reuse a scratch org, deploy current source into it, make a change, sync that change in the needed direction, then commit the result to Git — committing to Git is the final step that locks the change in as the new source of truth.
